Psychology from scratch

What psychology studies, its history, branches and methods.

Lesson 5. Common myths

1 · Lesson

Many ideas about the mind circulate as truths and are not. "We only use 10% of our brain": imaging shows activity throughout the brain over the day, and a small injury in almost any area has consequences. "People are left-brained or right-brained": the hemispheres have some specialisation, but they work together and there is no evidence that people fall into two types.

"Each person has a learning style (visual, auditory…) and learns better when taught in that style": this is one of the most widespread beliefs among teachers, but studies that have tested it have not found that benefit. "Memory works like a recording": remembering is reconstructing, and memories can change over time and with the questions we are asked.

Myths survive because they are simple, often repeated and sometimes contain a grain of truth. It is always worth asking where a claim comes from and what evidence supports it.

2 · Example

In the late 1990s the "Mozart effect" became popular: listening to Mozart would make babies smarter. The original study was with university students, measured one specific spatial task and the effect lasted a few minutes. Even so, CDs for babies were sold for years. It is a good example of how a small result grows as it is retold.

3 · Activity

Write down three sentences about the mind that you have heard many times. For each one, note what evidence would be needed to believe it. Then compare with what you have read in this lesson.
